source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2402.04494)
finding: A 270M-parameter transformer trained by supervised learning on Stockfish 16 labels, with no search at test time, plays at grandmaster level against humans. It is a pure one-pass pattern-to-move system, the machine analogue of recognition-primed choice.
numbers: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans, 2299 vs bots; puzzle accuracy 95.4% on 10K Lichess puzzles; 10M games, 15 billion annotated data points.
limits: Grandmaster claim holds only vs humans; the paper says the gap to Stockfish is not closed. Supervised distillation of a search engine, not self-discovered recognition.
agent_relevance: A single forward pass can carry expert-level move choice when the situation is in-distribution. Supports a fast first-option mode for familiar cases.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Table 1, model size scaling and baselines
finding: Bigger no-search models are better. A general instruction-tuned LLM reading PGN is much weaker than the chess-specific policy.
numbers: Puzzle acc: 9M 88.9%, 136M 94.5%, 270M 95.4%. Tournament Elo 2025, 2259, 2299. GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct: 66.5% puzzles, Lichess 1755 vs bots. Leela policy-only 88.6% puzzles.
limits: Different inputs (FEN vs PGN) and training (SL vs RL), so cross-agent comparison has caveats, as the authors state.
agent_relevance: Recognition quality depends on the amount of domain-specific experience. A general LLM has weaker built-in recognition than a specialist, so a scaffold should not assume strong intuition.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Section 4.1 and appendix on workarounds
finding: The no-search policy has stated blind spots: it cannot see threefold repetition because it has no game history, it cannot plan ahead to avoid being forced into repetition, and the authors say opponents may find weaknesses through repeated play because the policy is deterministic.
numbers: Workaround used: set the win percentage of a repetition-triggering move to 50% before the softmax. Elo drops from 2895 (humans) to 2299 (bots).
limits: Single model family; the bot-vs-human gap has three hypothesised causes that were not separated.
agent_relevance: Matches the RPD boundary condition that pure recognition fails when the relevant structure lies outside the current snapshot. The agent needs a check for history or long-range traps before committing.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Table 1, search versus no search for the same networks
finding: Adding search to the same networks lifts puzzle accuracy by a measurable margin. Search is most valuable where the fast policy is weakest.
numbers: AlphaZero: policy-only 56.1%, value-only 82.0%, 400 MCTS sims 95.6%. Leela: policy-only 88.6%, value-only 95.9%, 400 MCTS sims 99.6% (gain about 11 points over policy-only). Tournament Elo Leela 2292 policy-only vs 2858 with search.
limits: Puzzles are tactical and favour search; the differences are computed from the table by me.
agent_relevance: Gives a size for the cost of staying in fast mode: about 11 to 40 points of accuracy on hard tactical items. Useful when setting when to escalate.

source: Jenner et al. (2024) Evidence of Learned Look-Ahead in a Chess-Playing Neural Network (arXiv 2406.00877)
finding: Leela's policy network, one forward pass with no search, internally represents future optimal moves. Three lines of evidence: activation patching, attention heads moving information across time, and a probe.
numbers: Probe predicts the optimal move two turns ahead with 92% accuracy (in states with a single best line). Policy network rates over 2600 on Lichess. 22.5k puzzles kept from 900k.
limits: Puzzles filtered to ones Leela solves and a weaker Leela fails; many involve sacrifices. The paper calls it an existence proof, not a general account.
agent_relevance: Fast recognition may contain compressed simulation. RPD says experts mentally simulate the chosen option; a network may do something similar inside one pass, so fast mode need not be shallow.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent World Models and Latent Variable Estimation in Chess-Playing Language Models (COLM 2024, arXiv 2403.15498)
finding: A GPT trained only on next-character prediction of chess games learns an internal board state and estimates player skill as a latent variable. Adding a skill vector makes it play better.
numbers: Legal move rate 99.8% (16-layer), 99.6% (8-layer). Win rate vs Stockfish level 0: 46% (8-layer), 64% (16-layer). Best board-state probe 99.6% accuracy. Skill intervention raises win rate up to 2.6 times. Board-edit intervention success up to 92%.
limits: Small custom-trained models, not frontier LLMs; played against the weakest Stockfish level.
agent_relevance: Pattern recognition from text alone gives usable state and a read on who is playing. Suggests an agent can be steered by a skill or quality cue in its context.

source: Feng et al. (2023) ChessGPT: Bridging Policy Learning and Language Modeling (arXiv 2306.09200)
finding: General open LLMs track chess state poorly; training on chess game and language data fixes it. Recognition of position from move text is a learned, domain-specific skill.
numbers: BigBench chess state tracking, Real Short: LLaMA-7B 29.5%, RedPajama-Base 23.2%, ChessGPT-Base 99.5%, ChessGPT-Chat 98.5%. UCI-to-FEN Real Short: LLaMA 2.2%, ChessGPT-Base 95.1%.
limits: Task is state tracking, not move quality. Chat tuning slightly lowered synthetic long-game scores (92.8% to 85.1%).
agent_relevance: Experience in the domain format is what makes recognition work. An agent facing an unfamiliar format should not trust its first read.

source: McIlroy-Young et al. (2020) Aligning Superhuman AI with Human Behavior: Chess as a Model System (KDD 2020, arXiv 2006.01855)
finding: Strong engines predict human moves poorly. Maia, an AlphaZero-style network trained on human games per rating band, predicts human moves better and is tuned to a skill level.
numbers: Best Stockfish version scores at most 46% move matching; Maia's highest accuracy is over 52%; Maia accuracy around 50.8% to 52.9% across rating bands 1100 to 1900.
limits: Predicts the move played, not whether the move was good; online blitz-style data.
agent_relevance: What a human does in a familiar position is a different target from the best move. A recognition mode that imitates experts needs expert-like training data.

source: McIlroy-Young et al. (2020) Section 5 predicting errors
finding: A network can predict whether a human will make a large mistake on the next move, so failure of human fast choice is itself learnable.
numbers: Residual CNN 67.7% (board only) and 71.7% (with more input) vs fully connected 62.9% and 66.0% and random forest 56.4% and 63.0%.
limits: Blunder definition and sampling set by the authors; modest accuracy.
agent_relevance: Supports a learned monitor that flags when a quick choice is likely to be wrong, a model for the escalate trigger.

source: Tang et al. (2024) Maia-2: A Unified Model for Human-AI Alignment in Chess (arXiv 2409.20553)
finding: One skill-aware model replaces separate per-rating models and predicts human moves better and more coherently across skill levels.
numbers: Surpasses original Maia by almost 2 percentage points in move prediction accuracy; average perplexity 4.67 bits down to 4.07 bits.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read for numbers; full tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Expertise can be a continuous input rather than a switch, a hint for how an agent could condition its recognition on a competence estimate.

source: Monroe and Chalmers (2024) Mastering Chess with a Transformer Model (Chessformer, arXiv 2409.12272)
finding: Better position representation lets a transformer match no-search grandmaster-level play with far less compute. Policy-only play is strong at low cost.
numbers: CF-240M-policy Elo 2347, 93.5% puzzles, 12.8B FLOPS; GC-270M Elo 2299, 93.5%, 427B FLOPS; AlphaZero-policy Elo 1620, 61.0%; CF-240M-value Elo 2385, 97.6%, 256B FLOPS.
limits: Elo values for baselines taken from earlier papers; CF figures from the authors' own tournament.
agent_relevance: Fast recognition can be made cheap. About 33 times fewer FLOPS than GC-270M at equal puzzle accuracy is the efficiency argument for a first-option mode.

source: McGrath et al. (2022) Acquisition of Chess Knowledge in AlphaZero (PNAS, arXiv 2111.09259)
finding: Linear probes find many human chess concepts in AlphaZero's network. The paper maps what is learned when in training and where in depth, and reports the pattern repeats across training runs. Co-authored by a former world champion.
numbers: Concept probe results given as what-when-where plots; I read the abstract and introduction only and recorded no single headline figure.
limits: Probes show a concept can be decoded, not that the network uses it. Opening analysis done with one grandmaster.
agent_relevance: The expert pattern vocabulary (concepts) forms inside a recognition network. Hints that cue sets in an agent should be named human-level concepts.

source: Schut et al. (2023) Bridging the Human-AI Knowledge Gap: Concept Discovery and Transfer in AlphaZero (arXiv 2310.16410)
finding: Concepts extracted from AlphaZero were taught to four top grandmasters, who improved on the concept prototype positions. Expert recognition can be updated by new patterns from a machine.
numbers: 4 grandmasters; improvement reported in the abstract; I did not extract per-player scores.
limits: Very small human sample; positions chosen as prototypes of the concept.
agent_relevance: Pattern libraries can be extended after the fact; supports adding a retrievable store of vetted patterns rather than retraining.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: A Generative Agent with Fast and Slow Thinking for Complex Interactive Tasks (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2305.17390)
finding: An LLM agent with a small fast module that acts from learned associations and a slower LLM planner that is called only when needed beats prompt-only agents on ScienceWorld, with far fewer LLM tokens per action.
numbers: 30 ScienceWorld task types. Average score 84.7 vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3.
limits: Fast module is a fine-tuned small model trained on oracle paths; ScienceWorld only. Scores are the authors' own runs.
agent_relevance: The closest working LLM-agent version of RPD mode choice: act on the first workable option, escalate on trouble.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage, switching rule (method section and future work)
finding: The agent starts in fast mode and switches to the slow module on four triggers: stuck, invalid action, critical decision, unexpected observation. It returns to fast mode when the planned action buffer is empty. The authors list a trainable switching module as future work.
numbers: Stuck = K=5 consecutive steps with zero reward.
limits: Hand-written heuristic, not tuned or ablated per trigger in the parts I read.
agent_relevance: These four triggers are a ready test list for when the first workable option may fail. Matches RPD failure on novel or atypical situations.

source: Saha et al. (2025) System-1.x: Learning to Balance Fast and Slow Planning with Language Models (ICLR 2025, arXiv 2407.14414)
finding: A controller splits a planning problem into sub-goals, labels each easy or hard, and sends easy ones to a fast planner and hard ones to a search planner. A user parameter x sets the mix. The hybrid beats both pure modes at a fixed state-exploration budget.
numbers: On one of two tasks (Maze Navigation or Blocksworld; I did not confirm which in the text read): 70.4% valid plans at 13.6 states vs System-1 48.7% and System-2 37.2%. x=0.75 gives 75.7% at 16.6 states.
limits: Fine-tuned on search traces; two toy planning domains.
agent_relevance: Shows that routing by sub-goal difficulty beats a single global mode. Supports choosing mode per step rather than per task.

source: Su et al. (2025) Dualformer: Controllable Fast and Slow Thinking by Learning with Randomized Reasoning Traces (ICLR 2025, arXiv 2410.09918)
finding: One transformer trained with random dropping of reasoning trace parts can run fast, slow, or choose its own mode. Fast mode is far better than a solution-only model.
numbers: 30x30 maze: slow 97.6% optimal vs Searchformer 93.3% with 45.5% fewer steps; fast 80% vs solution-only 30%; auto 96.6% optimal with 59.9% fewer steps.
limits: Maze and Sokoban-type tasks; the math result was read in the abstract only.
agent_relevance: Self-chosen mode can cut reasoning steps by about 60% at small accuracy loss in a structured task, the efficiency case for mode choice.

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: Better Planning with Transformers via Search Dynamics Bootstrapping (Searchformer, arXiv 2402.14083)
finding: Training a transformer to emit the search trace of A* and then fine-tuning gives a planner that solves unseen puzzles and uses fewer search steps than the teacher.
numbers: 93.7% of unseen Sokoban puzzles solved optimally; up to 26.8% fewer search steps than A*; 5 to 10 times smaller model and 10 times smaller data than solution-only baselines.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; grid planning domains only.
agent_relevance: Search can be compressed into fast generation. Repeated search results can become next-time recognition.

source: Fang, Ma, Wang (2025) Thinkless: LLM Learns When to Think (arXiv 2505.13379)
finding: An LLM is trained with reinforcement learning to emit a short or think control token per query. A decoupled loss avoids the collapse seen with plain GRPO.
numbers: Cuts long-chain reasoning by 50% to 90% on Minerva Algebra, MATH-500, GSM8K while keeping accuracy (per abstract and results table).
limits: Math benchmarks only; difficulty judged by the model's own ability, so errors in self-assessment carry through.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a model can learn its own mode choice. Plain reward training collapsed to one mode, a failure case to avoid.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (arXiv 2212.05206)
finding: Early GPT-3 models give the intuitive wrong answer to Cognitive Reflection Test and semantic illusion items at human-like or higher rates. ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 avoid those errors.
numbers: Correct: GPT-3-davinci-003 5%, humans 38%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%. Intuitive wrong answers: davinci-003 80%, humans 55%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, ChatGPT-4 0%.
limits: Human comparison numbers come from the paper's own sample and prior human studies; possible training contamination.
agent_relevance: Models are not equally intuition-prone: weaker ones answer with the first workable option and are fooled by trap items, so mode choice should depend on model strength.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) chain-of-thought manipulations
finding: Forcing step-by-step reasoning moves a weak model away from intuition; blocking it hurts stronger models only a little.
numbers: Chain-of-thought prompt on GPT-3-davinci-003: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive wrong 80% to 29%. Blocking chain of thought: ChatGPT-4 correct 95% to 88%; ChatGPT-3.5 correct unchanged.
limits: Small item sets; chain-of-thought blocking may not be fully effective.
agent_relevance: A scaffold step that forces deliberation is worth most when the model's first answer is the trap answer.

source: Wen et al. (2024) DiLu: A Knowledge-Driven Approach to Autonomous Driving with Large Language Models (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2309.16292)
finding: A driving agent retrieves few-shot experiences similar to the current scene from a memory, reasons, and a reflection module stores safe or corrected decisions. This is recall of similar past cases, as in RPD.
numbers: With 40 memory items it matches RL methods trained over 600,000 episodes, and generalises better to diverse scenarios.
limits: Simulated highway driving; I did not extract the table of success rates.
agent_relevance: A working LLM loop built on retrieval of prior similar situations plus reflection. Suggests a case memory feeding the first option.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models (arXiv 2305.16291)
finding: An agent stores successful action programs in a skill library indexed by the embedding of their description and retrieves them for similar tasks, instead of replanning from scratch.
numbers: 3.3 times more unique items, 2.3 times longer distances, tech tree milestones up to 15.3 times faster than prior state of the art in Minecraft.
limits: Gains are for the whole system (curriculum, library, iterative prompting), not retrieval alone in the part I read.
agent_relevance: Pattern-to-action reuse inside an LLM loop; the skill library plays the role of an expert's learned repertoire.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning (arXiv 2303.11366)
finding: After a failed trial, the agent writes a verbal reflection and carries it into the next trial. A simple heuristic detects hallucination and inefficient planning to trigger a reset.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. ALFWorld: ReAct plus Reflexion completes 130 of 134 tasks; ReAct-only performance stalls between trials 6 and 7.
limits: Needs repeated attempts, which the paper itself notes can be impractical when actions are irreversible.
agent_relevance: An RPD-style check on a first option followed by repair; the cost is that it relies on retries.

source: Jenner et al. (2024) dataset construction and caveats
finding: The look-ahead finding was shown on a filtered set: puzzles a weaker Leela fails and the full Leela solves, which are more likely to need look-ahead, and in which the first move often sacrifices a piece.
numbers: 22.5k puzzles remain from 900k; the paper states results are weaker where the first and second move target squares differ.
limits: Selection could overstate how common look-ahead is across ordinary positions.
agent_relevance: Do not assume fast mode always includes simulation; test on ordinary cases too.
